topic: Running a meeting that ends with decisions
scope_note: Practical steps for the person running a recurring team or project meeting: before (name the decision, invite the right people), during (stay on it, park side topics, say how and by whom it is decided) and at the close (read back, then write it up). No meeting statistics, no decision science.

facts.statement: A meeting that is meant to produce a decision should have that decision named before it starts, in the invite or agenda.
facts.reference_hint: Antony Jay, 'How to Run a Meeting', Harvard Business Review (1976): the meeting needs a clear purpose and an agenda circulated beforehand.

facts.statement: Phrasing the decision as a question, for example 'Do we ship the pilot in May or June?', tells attendees what they must come ready to answer.
facts.caveat: This is common facilitation guidance rather than a tested law; say it as a practical tip, not as proof that it always works.
facts.reference_hint: Common agenda-writing guidance in management guides; no single study is claimed.

facts.statement: A topic title such as 'Pilot update' only names a subject; it does not tell people whether a decision is needed.
facts.caveat: Practical observation from agenda guidance; not a research finding.

facts.statement: Invite the people who are needed to make the decision, including whoever owns it, and the people whose input it cannot be made without.
facts.reference_hint: Antony Jay (1976), HBR: keep attendance to those who need to be there; Rogers and Blenko, 'Who Has the D?', HBR (2006), on clear decision roles.

facts.statement: Keeping the invite list to the people the decision needs tends to make a decision easier to reach than a larger group would.
facts.caveat: A rule of thumb from meeting guidance. Do not state a magic group size; the right size depends on the decision. People who only need to know the result can be sent the written summary instead.
facts.reference_hint: Antony Jay (1976), HBR; Steven Rogelberg, The Surprising Science of Meetings (2019), on inviting only those needed.

facts.statement: Before discussion starts, the person running the meeting restates the decision the meeting must make.
facts.caveat: Facilitation practice; no specific study is claimed.

facts.statement: A parking lot is a visible list, such as a corner of the board, where off-topic items are written down so the group can return to the decision and the item is not lost.
facts.reference_hint: Standard facilitation technique in meeting-management guides.

facts.statement: Parked items only help if someone is named to pick each one up afterwards, otherwise parking becomes a polite way to drop them.
facts.caveat: Practical judgement from facilitation guidance; say it as advice.

facts.statement: Before discussion, make clear how the decision will be made, for example the owner decides after hearing the group, or the group agrees by consensus or vote.
facts.caveat: Different decision rules suit different decisions; the lesson should not rank them or claim one is best.
facts.reference_hint: Rogers and Blenko, 'Who Has the D?', HBR (2006), on clarity about who decides.

facts.statement: Make clear who makes the decision, so one named person can call it when discussion ends.
facts.reference_hint: Rogers and Blenko, 'Who Has the D?', HBR (2006): decisions stall when roles are unclear.

facts.statement: Close the meeting by reading back each decision, with an owner and a due date, so people can correct it before they leave.
facts.reference_hint: Antony Jay (1976), HBR: record what was decided and who is to take action; reading back is standard facilitation practice.

facts.statement: A recorded decision states what was decided, who owns the follow-up, and by when. A line that only names a topic discussed, such as 'Discussed the pilot timeline', is not a decision.
facts.caveat: This is a practical working definition used in action-item guidance, not a formal standard.

facts.statement: Send the decisions and actions in writing soon after the meeting, ideally the same day, to attendees and anyone affected.
facts.caveat: 'Same day' is a practical recommendation, not a researched threshold; say 'soon after, ideally the same day'.
facts.reference_hint: Antony Jay (1976), HBR, on minutes recording decisions and actions; common in management guides.

facts.statement: The written summary lets people who were absent, and people who remember the meeting differently, check the same list of decisions, owners and dates.
facts.caveat: Plain reasoning from practice, not a measured effect.

terms.definition: The one named person who makes, or calls, the decision.
How the decision will be made, for example owner decides after hearing the group, or the group agrees.
A visible list of off-topic items to pick up later.
Saying each decision aloud at the close, with owner and due date.

not_claimed: Any figure for hours or money wasted in meetings, or the share of meetings that are unproductive; none is used.
That there is an ideal number of attendees (such as 7 or the two-pizza rule) backed by evidence.
That a particular day, time or length (such as 25 minutes) makes meetings better.
That any one decision rule (consensus, vote, owner decides) is best in general.
Any quote attributed to a named executive or author about meetings.
That standing meetings or shorter meetings fix the problem by themselves.
That people have learning styles that change how meetings should be run.
